Congressman Moore’s bill highlights a critical issue—342 officers shot in 2024 alone is unacceptable. But let’s be clear: throwing more bureaucracy at the problem isn’t the answer. The federal government already burns cash on absurdities like $75M contracts for website surveys and $3.5M for “cloud expertise consultants.” 

Redirect existing funds from bloated consulting contracts and DEI grants toward officer safety programs instead of creating new reporting layers. Every dollar spent on redundant data systems is a dollar not spent on bulletproof vests or mental health resources. Streamline existing budgets, enforce accountability for wasteful spending, and prioritize frontline needs over bureaucratic box-checking. 

If Washington can waste millions on diversity seminars, it can damn well protect cops without another bill.

The Improving Law Enforcement Officer Safety and Wellness Through Data Act (H.R. 2240) is a necessary step to address the surge in targeted violence against officers, with 60 felonious killings in 2022 alone and 30% from ambush attacks. Mandating DOJ reports on federal/state responses, training efficacy, and mental health impacts cuts through bureaucratic inertia to expose systemic failures. While collecting data on attacks like those analyzed in Section 3(a)(1)-(13) is critical, the real test is whether this leads to actionable reforms rather than another taxpayer-funded paper shuffle.

The bill’s focus on expanding protective gear distribution through the Patrick Leahy Bulletproof Vest Partnership (Section 3(a)(9)) must avoid becoming a slush fund for administrative overhead instead of frontline equipment. Law enforcement deserves more than performative “reports” – they need Congress to redirect the $55 million wasted annually on redundant DOJ grant programs into actual armor, trauma care, and vetted mental health resources.

Accountability starts with data, but ends with dismantling the red tape that leaves officers under-equipped and overexposed.

Passing H.R. 2240 proves Congress can prioritize frontline heroes over bureaucratic bloat when it wants. The bill’s 356-55 House vote shows even Democrats recognize the crisis of ambush attacks and mental health struggles plaguing law enforcement. But let’s be clear: this isn’t about throwing money at the problem. It’s about forcing DOJ to finally track the full scope of violence against officers - including the 30% killed in unprovoked attacks last year.

Real accountability starts with data, not performative “reforms.” Now watch how fast the same politicians who backed this bill turn around and underfund the bulletproof vest program in the next omnibus.

Support cops with facts and armor, not empty rhetoric.
